articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Spoilers for VisionQuest follow. The prospect of having to watch past movies and TV shows to fully understand or appreciate the stories of new ones is often cited as one of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s problems by detractors. On the other hand, for many of the franchise’s fans, revisiting previous tales in preparation for new ones is great fun. Marvel and Disney are fully aware of this, and have curated a special “Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday ,” collection of titles on Disney+, with the latter group in mind. The films and TV shows deemed the most important precursors to Doomsday are marked by distinctive green outlines around their thumbnails on the streaming service, with the exceptions of especially recent releases like VisionQuest and Avengers: Endgame Encore . The existing collection is already pretty thorough, but fans looking for an even more comprehensive trip down memory lane could also add the following titles to their rewatching schedules.

Loki’s (Tom Hiddleston) two-season TV spin-off is one of the most influential projects in Marvel’s Multiverse Saga, and as such is naturally one of the titles included in Disney’s Doomsday playlist. And Thor (Chris Hemsworth) is of course a leading character in the three previous Avengers movies that are also included. But with both Asgardian brothers seemingly set to play key roles in Doomsday , it makes sense for viewers to go back even further to the film that introduced them and their always complicated relationship. Kenneth Branagh’s Thor is often underappreciated for how effectively it introduced the fantastical Asgardian mythology into the more realistic world established by the MCU’s earliest films, and revisiting it ahead of Doomsday will emphasize how far the franchise and the characters have come. Returning to the beginning of Hemsworth and Hiddleston’s Marvel tenures reminds the viewer how consistently excellent the work they’ve done over the last fifteen years has been and will make Thor and Loki’s scenes in Doomsday , which will hopefully include a brotherly reunion, even more emotional.

The return of cast members from the original trilogy of X-Men films, which predate the MCU itself, is one of Doomsday ’s biggest selling points, and the 20th Century Fox franchise’s first two movies are already on Disney’s playlist. But fans are unlikely to pass on the excuse to also rewatch this powerful later entry in the series. Although not technically a multiverse film, Days of Future Past certainly feels like a spiritual precursor to the current MCU saga, as it brought together the original X-Men cast and their younger counterparts introduced in the 1960s period prequel X-Men: First Class , several years before the MCU first featured time travel in Avengers: Endgame .

Based on an iconic comic book arc of the same name, the film features the surviving original X-Men sending Logan/Wolverine’s (Hugh Jackman) mind back in time into the body of his younger self to alter the past in the hopes of preventing a dystopian future in which mutants have been hunted to near extinction. None of the members of the First Class cast have been announced as returning for Doomsday or Avengers: Secret Wars (though Days of Future Past ’s Quicksilver, Evan Peters, has already played an infamous role in the Multiverse Saga) and it’s unclear if the upcoming movies will be closely adhering to the continuity of any past X-Men entries other than the MCU’s own Deadpool & Wolverine . But if any of that continuity is to be respected, it makes sense to have the X-Men’s Doomsday arc take place after the optimistic, timeline-altering ending of Days of Future Past , which explains how characters like the older Charles Xavier/Professor X (Sir Patrick Stewart) and Scott Summers/Cyclops (James Marsden) can appear in the new film after being killed off in earlier ones. Days of Future Past is also the only movie so far to feature Sentinels, the mutant-hunting robots also returning in Doomsday , in a significant role.

Jackman’s return in Deadpool & Wolverine was controversial given that he’d already killed off a version of Logan in this critically acclaimed, R-rated spin-off. But despite all the jokes at its expense, the 2024 film did successfully introduce a new version of the character for Jackman to play while still honoring its predecessor’s legacy. The death of the previous Logan inspires the new variant, as well as Wade Wilson/Deadpool (Ryan Reynolds) and the deceased Logan’s cloned daughter, Laura/X-23 (Dafne Keen) to return to heroism despite their respective personal demons. Wade and the new Logan are all but confirmed to appear in Doomsday , with many fans expecting them to play even larger roles in Secret Wars , and it wouldn’t be surprising if Laura also reappears in one or both movies, so the revered film that introduced her and features her father’s death is an easy choice for addition to rewatch playlists. As with Doomsday itself, however, the recent death of Stewart, who appears as another ill-fated variant of Charles, will make Logan even more emotionally draining to watch going forward.

None of the members of the superhuman Maximoff family featured in VisionQuest have been officially cast in Doomsday or Secret Wars , though the series’ explosive post-credits scene effectively guarantees that matriarch Wanda Maximoff/The Scarlet Witch (Elizabeth Olsen) will be in at least one of the two. But it’s seeming increasingly likely that Wanda reuniting with Vision (Paul Bettany) and their sons Billy (Joe Locke) and Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) will be a storyline in the Avengers duology. Given that, it’s surprising that the earlier series that introduced the boys and was the last project to feature all four family members onscreen together isn’t included in Marvel’s official playlist. WandaVision was also the first project released as part of the Multiverse Saga and is arguably its best exploration of grief, a theme that has connected many of the saga’s installments, making it a natural addition to Doomsday (and Secret Wars ) prep.

Which Marvel projects are you rewatching before Doomsday ? Discuss in the comments.

Italy ’s RAI Cinema and Leone Film Group have acquired exclusive Italian distribution rights for Mel Gibson ’s two-part biblical drama sequel, "The Resurrection of the Christ," from Lionsgate.

More than 20 years ago, Gibson shot the original “The Passion of the Christ” at Italy's Cinecittà studios in Rome. It became one of the largest-grossing independent films of all time with a worldwide box office of $610 million. The follow-up has been split into two movies, with “Part One” set to debut in U.S. theatres on May 6, 2027 and “Part Two” scheduled for May 25, 2028. Each installment will open in theaters on Ascension Day, a Christian holiday that celebrates the ascension of Jesus into heaven.

The project "explores the period between the crucifixion and the resurrection, employing a narrative that encompasses both symbolic and spiritual dimensions, underscored by a powerful and evocative visual style," according to a statement from RAI Cinema. The broadcaster's banner 01 Distribution will replicate Lionsgate's release pattern day-and-date in Italy.

“The Passion of the Christ” followed Jim Caviezel as Jesus of Nazareth and Monica Bellucci as Mary Magdalene in the final 12 hours before the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.

Gibson has described the sequels as an “acid trip,” adding that he “never read anything like” the scripts, which the filmmaker has been writing alongside Randall Wallace. Finnish actor Jaakko Ohtonen (“The Last Kingdom”) has replaced Caviezel in the role of Jesus with Mariela Garriga taking over from Monica Bellucci as Magdalene. articles.title: ‘Best Pancakes in the County’ Review: Nicolas Cage Stars in a Thriller You Could Fairly Describe as Tarantino Lite
articles.summary: From “The Petrified Forest” to “When You Comin’ Back, Red Ryder?” to “Albino Alligator” and beyond, playwrights and filmmakers have long relied on the same claustrophobic premise: Disparate characters are stranded in a diner and pushed to extremes by cold-blooded, gun-toting bad guys. (OK, “Albino Alligator” actually was set in a New Orleans bar, but […]
articles.content:
From “The Petrified Forest” to “When You Comin’ Back, Red Ryder?” to “Albino Alligator” and beyond, playwrights and filmmakers have long relied on the same claustrophobic premise: Disparate characters are stranded in a diner and pushed to extremes by cold-blooded, gun-toting bad guys. (OK, “Albino Alligator” actually was set in a New Orleans bar, but close enough.) In “ Best Pancakes in the County ,” writer-director Ken Sanzel laces this whiskery setup with the seriocomic violence and show-offy wordplay one might expect of someone who repeatedly watched early Quentin Tarantino movies, slapped their forehead, and exclaimed: “Hey, I can do that!” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize 'Woman Unknown' Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: 'Everything Is Open'

One of two new releases this week showcasing Nicolas Cage in not-entirely-convincing prosthetics (the other being the sports-centric biopic “Madden”), “Pancakes” has the Oscar-winning and profligately prolific actor cast as a cunning criminal known as S.O.B. — no joke, that’s how he’s referenced by others and identified in the closing credits — who’s introduced while cracking a safe supposedly stuffed with $11 million in an FBI stash house. When he discovers that his partner in crime lied about how much loot was there, S.O.B. expresses his disappointment nonverbally. But he holds on to another item in the safe, a hard drive that more or less serves as the movie’s propulsive McGuffin.

After that, Cage, sporting garish ‘70s attire and a fake upturned nose that recalls Christina Ricci’s exaggerated snout in “Penelope,” drops out of sight for a stretch, one of his sporadic disappearing acts in the movie. The narrative slack is taken up (for a while, at least) by the interactions of vaguely defined Tarantinoesque cosplayers at a remote roadside diner that boasts… well, take another look at the title. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Two heavily armed groups arrive and repeatedly indicate they’re only one insult or cross look away from blasting each other as they await the arrival of S.O.B. On one side, we have hired guns led by Ryder (Ravi Patel), an S.O.B. functionary; on the other, some rogue FBI agents (helpfully identified as “thoroughly corrupt” by an on-screen legend) commanded by a tough cookie named Margot (Lauren German). Caught in the middle are the diner’s only two employees: Cookie (Justin Long), a fry cook who does his best to keep his head down by preparing food for his unwelcome guests, and Dolly (Shelley Henning), a brassy young waitress who dutifully serves the gun-toting customers while clearly plotting her next move.

Actually, both Dolly and Cookie aren't quite who they appear to be — which isn’t altogether surprising, given the incongruous calm they display in high-stress situations. Both characters figure prominently during the best-crafted sequence in “Pancakes,” where editors Magnus Häll and Håkan Karlsson deftly cut back and forth between two different hand-to-hand (or face-to-deep-fryer) battles. This montage is all the more impressive compared to the clumsily staged, borderline incoherent violence sprinkled throughout the rest of the movie.

Since this is “Best Pancakes in the County” and not “Waiting for Godot,” S.O.B. eventually arrives at the diner, giving Cage yet another chance to dial it up to 11 while devouring scenery with his customary fervor. A little bit of this goes a long way; a lot, alas, is par for the course from Cage these days.

On the other hand, many of the bigger laughs come from a few of Cage’s relatively understated co-stars. Brandon Mychal Smith’s deadpan incredulity as a corrupt agent is undeniably comical as he sincerely questions the veracity of the menu’s motto. (“Best pancakes in the county? What, were they reviewed somewhere? Food Network or something?”) And Long’s sad-sack demeanor as Cookie enables him to generate as much sympathy as amusement.

But there’s no getting around the fact that far too much of “Best Pancakes in the County” is taken up with faux-Tarantino dialogue riffs and overcompensating posing. It’s almost bad enough to give you indigestion while you stifle the occasional yawn.

articles.title: Batman Is the Dark Knight but These 5 Times He Was a Symbol of Hope (Including Gotham's Darkest Moment)
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics Everyone has a certain idea of who Batman is. He's the Dark Knight and he never smiles. He's the black avenger of Gotham City, the member of the Justice League that everyone is a little scared of. Back in post-Crisis DC, he would often be portrayed in group shots in shadow, the mysterious warrior who […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Everyone has a certain idea of who Batman is. He's the Dark Knight and he never smiles. He's the black avenger of Gotham City, the member of the Justice League that everyone is a little scared of. Back in post- Crisis DC, he would often be portrayed in group shots in shadow, the mysterious warrior who showed up, saved the day, and left because the Joker escaped from Arkham again. He has an aura of competence that few heroes can match, but he keeps everyone at arm's reach. He has no qualms with using fear to keep the criminals of Gotham in line; he's not going to kill you, but you're probably going to wish he did.

Batman is a symbol for a lot of things, but one thing that he's not associated with often is hope.; that's Superman's game. However, when it comes right down to it, Batman is all about hope. He's the one that everyone looks to when the day needs saving and there have been numerous times that the Caped Crusader showing up was a moment of hope. Batman was a symbol of hope these five times, proving that he's more than just the night's most dangerous hero.

We talk about "Death of Superman" a lot when we talk about '90s DC and what the various Super-events meant for the character. However, other than "Knightfall", we don't really talk very much about the Dark Knight in the '90s. Much like the Man of Steel, he had numerous big event stories, with Gotham ravaged by the Clench plague and a massive earthquake. All of this led the federal government deciding to cut Gotham off from the rest of the country at the end of the decade. The city is cut off from the mainland, left to its own devices. This is the reality of "No Man's Land", a year long Batman epic that ran through every Bat-related comic of 1999 and 2000 (I'm pretty sure it's close to a hundred parts if you include all the tie-ins).

This being Gotham, the city broke down completely, with the various gangs carving out their own fiefdoms. Gotham was no more and even Batman had seemingly given up, with the rest of the Bat-Family scrambling to make a difference. When the Dark Knight started fighting again, he was a rallying symbol of the old order, allowing the Bat-Family and the GCPD to take back the city. Batman brought hope to the hopeless, allowing the city to survive.

Tom King's Batman run gets a lot of hate that I don't agree with whatsoever. Not only did he build an 85-issue plot that cemented Bane as one of Batman's greatest foes, but was able to tell numerous great Batman stories, all while digging into the psychology of the character. It all led to "City of Bane". Throughout the run, Bane had been manipulating events to take away everything from the Caped Crusader, using the Psycho-Pirate to take control of Gotham City, creating an army of villains to use as his lieutenants. He had Alfred hostage, promising to kill him if Batman or the Bat-Family re-entered the city.

Beaten mentally and physically, he goes to Catwoman for help and eventually the two of them make their way back to the city. The Dark Knight re-entering the city was the sign for the rest of the Bat-Family to make their move, leading to the end of Bane's reign. While the whole thing cost Alfred his life – Damian had tried to attack the city before Batman returned, leading to his death – Bats and company would defeat Bane and the Flashpoint Batman (who had decided to work with Bane because the villain would make sure that Batman no longer existed and Bruce could finally have a life), saving the city and getting everything back to normal.

Kingdom Come , by Mark Waid and Alex Ross, is one of the greatest stories in DC history. It took place in an alternate future where Superman's retirement led the rest of his generation of heroes to take off their costumes, replaced by a more violent new breed. However, there was one who didn't quit and no one was surprised – Batman. He kept up his war on crime in Gotham, using Bat-Robots to create a police state. The return of Superman and the Justice League was just another problem he had to deal with and he did it by teaming up with League's enemies, ostensibly because they were more human, all in an attempt to figure out what Lex Luthor's plan was and how to stop it. However, he was unable to take down Billy Batson before he became Captain Marvel and Luthor's plan to start a rebellion at the Justice League's Gulag was set in motion.

Wonder Woman led the Justice League's forces against the imprisoned metahumans, but they were slowly but surely overwhelmed. Into this hopeless battle dropped Batman and his crew. Clad in armor that shored up his aged, battered body, the Dark Knight's entrance was a turning point in the battle and one of the biggest aura-farming moments in comics, made all the better by Alex Ross's gorgeous art. Kingdom Come is full of amazing moments , but this one will always be one of the best.

Bruce Wayne became Batman because of the worst night you can imagine, watching as his parents bled out on the cold concrete. He vowed to make sure that no one would feel what he felt that night; noble but a fool's errand for the all-too human Wayne. Eventually, he had the misfortune of witnessing someone go through the exact same thing as he did and stepped in. Dick Grayson lost his parents to crime, but gained a new family thanks to Bruce. He saw a kindred spirit in the boy, leading to him becoming Robin the Boy Wonder. Dick would go down as the greatest sidekick of them all, founding the Teen Titans, and eventually becoming Nightwing.

As Nightwing, Dick proved that he had more than learned the lessons of being a superhero from his mentor. Grayson was first given a chance to take on the mantle of the Dark Knight after Bruce defeated Azrael, a short stint that most fans barely recall. However, after Batman's "death" in Final Crisis , Dick would end up becoming the Caped Crusader again. He was a very different hero and became another kind of Batman, one who was all smiles and saving the day and being nice to his fellow heroes. He had a much more hopeful aura than his mentor, showing that Batman could be more than just the grim avenger of the night.

The Justice League is DC's greatest team , with Batman as one of the guiding lights of the group since the beginning. Over the years, he's gained a reputation with them; while he's often short with his teammates, he's the guy who saves the day more often than not. He's been known to show up when things are at their worst, bringing with him the key to saving the day, giving the more powerful members a chance to make a difference. The League knows that when Batman shows up when things are at their worst, they're about to get a whole lot better and one of the best examples of this came in JLA #3.

The Hyperclan were a new team of proactive heroes, calling the Justice League old-fashioned and taking the esteem of the public from them with their flashy yet empty superheroics. Eventually the two teams end up fighting, with the Hyperclan trouncing the League rather easily. Everyone is taken down, except Batman. He's able to figure out the Hyperclan's secret – that they're White Martians, meaning that they're weak to fire. He used this to break their hole on the League, which led to the heroes winning the day. The Caped Crusader showed up when the League was at their lowest and saved the day, showing that sometimes, hope wears black.

Do you think Batman works as a symbol of hope? Any moments you would have wanted to see on this list? Sound off in the comment section below.

"I’m about to work with Jesse on a movie — he wrote something," he told the U.K.'s Heart Breakfast radio on […]
articles.content:
Kieran Culkin has let slip that he's reuniting with Jesse Armstrong for the first time since " Succession " came to an end three years ago — but that it's got nothing to do with Roman Roy.

"I’m about to work with Jesse on a movie — he wrote something," he told the U.K.'s Heart Breakfast radio on Friday, without revealing any further details.

Armstrong doesn't currently have any announced films in development. His last feature "Mountainhead" — which he wrote and was also his directorial debut — released on Apple, while A24's "Jonty," which he co-wrote with his "Peep Show" co-creator Sam Bain and stars Jesse Plemons and Cole Escola, is currently in post-production. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize 'Woman Unknown' Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: 'Everything Is Open'

Since losing out in the battle for Waystar at the end of "Succession" and saying goodbye to his Emmy-winning spell as the Roy family's most foul-mouthed and emotionally chaotic heir, Culkin has become a major movie force. He won the best supporting Oscar for Jesse Eisenberg's "A Real Pain" and is currently in cinemas as the younger Caesar Flickerman for franchise prequel "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." Next year, he's due to appear in Warner Bros.' untitled Nancy Meyers rom-com alongside Erin Doherty and Jude Law.

For all his move into starry, studio tentpoles, "Succession" fans will likely relish the chance to see Culkin back with the writer who gave him his most memorable role, a role he said he himself missed.

"It was a great show. I miss that whole thing," he said. "It was a lot of fun because I decided early on, this is a guy who’s never had to suffer consequences in his life. He can just talk his way in and out of any situation, like how fun is that to play! Completely unhinged." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Returning to what he told Variety in an interview in 2023, Culkin also noted that Armstrong had discussed another season of "Succession" with him.

"He pitched me three different of what season 5 could be, they all sounded good," he said. "But it ended perfectly. The way it was supposed to."

articles.content:
EXCLUSIVE: DramaBox 's latest microdrama original will be set around an Indian wedding.

3 Days Till I Do is now playing on the vertical video app. Commissioned by car manufacturer Toyota and its Asian American advertising agency, Intertrend Communications, this marks the latest example of a brand commissioning a full production to hit its consumer base.

articles.title: ‘The Big Boom!’: Doc About a Bulgarian Village With a Massive Weapons Factory ‘Anticipates the Future World We'll Inhabit’

Stalin”) is set in Kazanlak, Bulgaria’s Valley of Roses, where the sounds of explosions often disrupt an otherwise peaceful village. These come from the Arsenal factory, which employs 10,000+ people to produce […]
articles.content:
IDFA Frontlight title “The Big Boom!” is rife with contrasts. The fifth documentary from Swiss filmmaker Gabriel Tejedor (“Svetlana: My Father is J. Stalin”) is set in Kazanlak, Bulgaria’s Valley of Roses, where the sounds of explosions often disrupt an otherwise peaceful village. These come from the Arsenal factory, which employs 10,000+ people to produce weapons and ammunition that are mostly sent to Ukraine ’s frontlines, just a few miles away. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For many residents, the overriding question is how to reconcile this multi-billion-dollar business and the jobs it generates and a brutal war that has devastated lives, homes and communities.

“It’s sad to say but thanks to this war we live very well,” says one resident. “Arsenal guarantees me job security and peace of mind,” says another. Meanwhile, a group of pacifists stage a protest against a monument to a historical figure responsible for the deaths of thousands of Bulgarians.

Given Kazanlak’s deep historical and cultural ties to Russia, many of them harbor mixed feelings about the country their work now opposes.

“The Big Boom!,” to which Lightdox acquired world sales rights in October, follows four residents whose lives are impacted by the looming factory in different ways: A factory worker who takes pride in her work and feels empowered as she refines her shooting skills; a former Arsenal employee turned pacifist journalist who left the factory decades ago and now challenges perspectives about the war; a Ukrainian refugee and his daughter rebuilding their lives in Kazanlak while dealing with the trauma of loss. And lastly, a Roma grandmother whose family history bears the painful memories and lingering consequences of the factory’s past. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“The Big Boom!” is produced by Mira Film Basel GmbH, and is co-produced by RTS Radio Télévision Suisse and SRG SSR, with the support of Swiss and regional film funds and cultural institutions. Susanna Guggenberger of Mira Film produced the doc.

Tejedor discusses his own conflicted feelings about what pacifism really portends:

How has the war in Ukraine changed your idea of pacifism, especially for you who grew up in Switzerland? Can someone still be a pacifist in a world where weapons seem necessary to defend peace?

I come from Switzerland, where neutrality is almost part of our national identity. I'm 47, and I've never had a war close to me. During the Yugoslav Wars, I was too young to really feel concerned. But now it's different. Ukraine is just a few hundred kilometers away. Of course, I'm against weapons, but I also deeply support Ukraine. In Bulgaria, I discovered that if you call yourself a pacifist, people can understand that as being pro-Russian, because you want to leave things as they are. That made me question my own understanding of pacifism. Beyond Ukraine, the film looks at a global scale: the future world we'll inhabit and the looming threat of a WWIII.

Kazanlak is a town where everyday life exists alongside a major weapons factory. How did getting to know the people and the town change the way you see this relationship?

Kazanlak is in the Rose Valley, famous for its roses and perfume. When I first came across Arsenal, I found the contrast extraordinary. Yet spending time there, I saw the factory isn't separate from daily life - it shapes the local economy, history and identity. Weapons are everywhere: shooting ranges, arms fairs, military events. Still, Kazanlak doesn't fully embrace its arms industry, using its rose heritage to soften its image. Meanwhile, people raise children and live ordinary lives. I became drawn to this coexistence, rather than viewing the factory simply as a place where weapons are made.

Your four protagonists have very different views about Arsenal. What did their stories teach you about the difficult choices people face when their work is connected to war?

I wanted very different protagonists, not only Arsenal workers. Some are pacifists; others are enthusiastic about weapons. Some see Arsenal as a way to afford a seaside holiday, while others call it prostitution. Some are fatalistic, believing humans will inevitably fight. I didn't want to judge these positions, only ask the audience: What would you do in this town? Where do you stand on weapons? Arsenal is everywhere - in schools, in cultural life - making it genuinely hard to simply say, “No, I won't work there.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Throughout the film, you also question your own role in the conflict. Did making this film change the way you think about your own responsibility for war, and do you still consider yourself a pacifist?

From the beginning of the war in Ukraine, I realized I was playing a role too - buying Russian products like oil, gas and wheat, or living in a country that manufactures weapons for Ukraine, just like Bulgaria. I cannot look at Bulgaria as if it were only their problem; we are all involved. As a pacifist, my position on weapons has changed, yes. Still, weapons aren't the only answer: Europe must develop renewable energies to stop funding the Russian state and sanctions should target anyone aiding the Russian military complex, not just Russians and Belarusians.

articles.content:
The Criterion Channel has acquired three short films by the London-based Nigerian British filmmaker Tomisin Adepeju .

The three films, Appreciation (2019), Journey Mercies (2023), and Lift Me Up (2026), will be available to stream on Criterion from December 1.

Adepeju wrote and directed each of the shorts, which were produced in London and feature both English and Yoruba language dialogue.

“I tried to look this up, but I don’t think there are any other Yoruba films in the collection,” Adepeju told Deadline in an interview ahead of the acquisition announcement. “As a diasporic filmmaker, I hope this means there'll be more films by British Nigerian filmmakers included. It's a dream come true. It really is surreal.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News David Lean Doc Narrated By Cate Blanchett Sells To Spain, France, Germany, Australia Ahead Of UK Release News Doha Film Festival Lifts Off As Gulf States Remain On High Alert Amid Iran Attacks

Adepeju is a popular figure across the UK industry. His shorts have screened at Sundance, the BFI London Film Festival and the London Short Film Festival. He is also known for his influential screening programme and workshop series Dailies , which runs monthly across London. “As a filmmaker, you're trying to make your films and get them seen. But I realised other artists like me want to learn more about the craft of filmmaking, network, and meet like-minded people,” Adepeju says about the initial idea behind Dailies. “Initially, it was just about showing films. I curated monthly screenings of shorts and features, anchored by discussions with filmmakers about their work and craft. Through that, people could meet others and be inspired to make their own work.”

Dailies has now been running for four years. Previous speakers at Dailies events include Mia Bays, former director of the BFI Filmmaking Fund, Farhana Bhula, director of Film4, and Eva Yates, director of BBC Film. Films screened at Dailies include Akinola Davies Jr.'s My Father’s Shadow, Savanah Leaf's Earth Mama , and Boris Lojkine's Souleymane’s Story .

Adepeju adds, “Dailies is also now informing my practice, and vice versa. Through these events, I'm meeting commissioners, casting directors, and producers. It's been incredible, really nice to have the two work side by side.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Adepeju says his narrative fiction work is largely shaped by questions of identity, “exploring who you are and what informs your character, your faith, and your relationships,” particularly in relation to Nigerians in the diaspora, but not exclusively.

“I was inspired by growing up watching films by Jean-Luc Godard, Bergman, and Ozu—world cinema, really. Those films were culturally specific, but they also encompassed universal themes,” he says.

“In the same way, I'm making films about Nigerians in the diaspora, particularly in South London, and the themes and issues that shape their lives: grief, love, death, identity, and all of those things. That's what binds the three films together. They're culturally rooted in South London, but they're about universal issues that, regardless of where you're from, I hope you can see the humanity in.”

Earlier this year, Adepeju completed a new short titled It's dancing time for BBC Film, produced by Jack Thomas-O'Brien of Sixteen Films. Adepeju is also in development on a feature, also to be produced by Thomas-O'Brien, with the BFI on board.

“The feature explores the same themes as my other work, but it's exciting to work on a longer-form piece. Ultimately, that's what I've been working towards for the past five or six years,” Adepeju says.

“I've been inspired by friends of mine, like Akinola Davies Jr., who made My Father's Shadow . I programmed his short film Lizard , and then we screened his feature early this year. I've screened It's What's Inside by Charlotte Regan and Last Swim by Sasha Nathwani. There have been so many great first features, especially by British directors. Seeing and programming all this work is inspiring, and it has definitely informed my own first feature.”

Adepeju jokes that he aims to get his feature out while there is still a significant buzz around films directed by British-Nigerians, with filmmakers like Davies Jr. and Olive Nwosu ( Lady , 2026) debuting features at major festivals.

“Olive's film was made with Film4 and the BFI. Akin's was made with BBC Film and the BFI. These institutions are now supporting us to make our work, which is timely, urgent, important, and well-crafted,” Adepeju says.

Appreciation (2019), Journey Mercies (2023), and Lift Me Up (2026) will be available to stream on the Criterion Channel from December 1.

articles.title: Social Media Bans in Tallinn Focus: Should Film Studios and Marketers Panic?
articles.summary: A National Research Group expert shared data on the impact of Australia's social media ban on movie-going among young audiences and discussed the planned U.K. launch of a similar initiative.
articles.content:
Australia has banned social media for people under the age of 16. A similar ban is set to hit the U.K. in 2027. And the European Union is talking about potential similar initiatives. So what is the impact on the film industry?

After all, Gen Z and Gen Alpha audiences have been key box-office drivers, and short social media videos and memes have helped make some movies into must-see cultural moments. So, what happens when young audiences are blocked from social media discovery? And how could these restrictions reshape the discovery and engagement with cinema? Or put differently: Should studios and marketers panic? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies "Learn From the Mistakes of Mentors": The Head of Tallinn's Discovery Campus Is All About Bridging Film Education and Industry Movies 'Sh*t Happens' Is Full of Dark Humor, But Its Director Knows It Will Cause a Stink in the DR

Given all these questions, the Just Film Industry Days program of the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event (ITBE) market featured a well-attended Friday session entitled “The New Underground: Film Discovery in the Age of Social Media Restrictions.”

Fergus Navaratnam-Blair, a researcher covering trends in media, entertainment, and technology who manages thought leadership for National Research Group, said that the U.K. social media restrictions would be "more far-reaching" than the ones in Australia.

Of course, banning social media usage and time "could create more time for kids and teens to spend at the cinema," he said. And indeed, a U.K. survey found that 42 percent of kids said they may spend more time watching films in movie theaters once the ban hits. Navaratnam-Blair also shared data showing that 25 percent of kids in Australia said that they have actually watched more movies in cinemas since the ban in the country started, even though the survey didn't detail how many more. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Also, in-home entertainment experienced a bigger boost, with 42 percent of respondents mentioning more home watching of movies and 39 percent mentioning more TV viewing at home.

What kinds of movie-going experiences will draw young audiences in an age of social media bans? Navaratnam-Blair had this to offer: "In a post-social world, it will be even more important to offer younger audiences truly unique live experiences," including premium large-format screenings, 2D or virtual reality screenings and screenings featuring special effects, such as wind, lights and seat movement.

One key question is, of course, if bans are effective. The expert shared that research has found that around 70 percent of Australians under the age of 16 still have social media access, according to their parents, whether through platforms that are not banned, such as Roblox or Discord, or by setting up accounts via VPNs or under different people's names.

All that is likely a blueprint for how things will be in the U.K. and potential future bans going into effect elsewhere. Concluded Navaratnam-Blair: "I do think there's going to be a subversion of the ban itself."

articles.title: Disney's Forgotten Sci-fi Franchise Is Gloriously Weird, And Was One of Kurt Russell's First Roles
articles.summary: Once upon a time, Disney would take a crazy idea and turn it into a charming family film. It could be about a spy dog, a professor who invents something that's out of this world, or a college kid who gets zapped by electricity and turns into the brightest person in the room. As a […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Once upon a time, Disney would take a crazy idea and turn it into a charming family film. It could be about a spy dog, a professor who invents something that's out of this world, or a college kid who gets zapped by electricity and turns into the brightest person in the room. As a matter of fact, Disney actually pulled this last idea off with one of their early films. And it starred an actor who would go on to become a favorite in millions of homes.

That's part of what makes the movie so interesting—it seamlessly weaves together elements of campus humor, sci-fi, and an unexpectedly crooked crime story. By the time the opening credits roll, the premise itself is intriguing. How much can one brain possibly store? What kind of chaos would result if the wrong people stumbled upon that information? And why is no one at this college concerned about the risk of frying their brain? All this is explained in one of Disney's offbeat live-action comedies, starring an early appearance by Kurt Russell.

Watching this movie, you’ll spend a fun and humorous college year with Kurt Russell as Dexter Riley in this classic Disney production. Dexter is a typical college student at Medfield College, but things start to go wrong when students persuade a wealthy businessman to give them an outdated computer. A seemingly little electrical shock followed by a wild electrical storm results in Dexter gaining the computer's knowledge. Now the everyday college student has become a walking encyclopedia, which is quite a change for what was probably a sub-par student last week.

Disney manages to avoid the idea of Dexter's strange new intelligence as just another superpower. His knowledge becomes a double-edged sword instead. Dean Higgins takes the opportunity to boost the college, while Dexter's friends cope with their own super-schoolboy. Meanwhile, the computer's other owner has considerably darker concerns about what Dexter might have discovered. Cesar Romero plays the businessman, and you'll never get to actually like him, but he keeps the right degree of diabolical class to keep you entertained by his crimes. It all gets into a very effective comedy engine: Dexter can answer any question, but as his own knowledge increases, so do his own doubts.

There's a certain nostalgia and idiosyncrasy to Disney's old Medfield College movies. They took college campuses and surrounded students with extraordinary scientific nonsense. Surprisingly, The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes began a trilogy that continued with Now You See Him, Now You Don't in 1972 and The Strongest Man in the World in 1975, with Russell as Dexter once more. The recipe is simple: give a gaggle of college students some amazing scientific invention, and watch as their everyday academic shenanigans turn into disaster. Honestly, it's a perfect recipe for family comedy.

Here's a quick little preview from Disney if you haven't had the chance to watch the full movie yet:

As you can probably tell, Russell makes the original film all the better by giving Dexter an easygoing charisma that keeps him relatable, rather than turning him into a lovable pain in the behind. That's important here, because the humor comes from getting to see some schlub struggle with all this. Way back before you'd ever seen him in Escape from New York or The Thing , Russell demonstrated that he could carry a Disney film. This one is far from being hard sci-fi, with computers that look frickin' ancient, and the plot gets dumber the longer you think about it. That's part of what makes it work. Disney latched onto a ludicrous premise and then built a cute little franchise with it. Sometimes the best forgotten films are the ones where they didn't take themselves too seriously.

These days, getting a computer's worth of knowledge from an electrical shock would probably land you in the emergency room, not a college Hall of Fame. But that's the magic of old-school Disney! Have you seen The Computer Wore Tennis Shoes , and do you think Kurt Russell's Dexter Riley deserves more recognition? Share your thoughts in the comments below. And tell us which forgotten Disney classic deserves a comeback!

articles.title: 5 Justice League Unlimited Villains I'm Still Waiting to See on the Big Screen in the DCU
articles.summary: Following the change in leadership, priorities for the DCU and future projects have shifted. David Ellison has expressed an interest in a fast-tracked Justice League, wanting Wonder Woman, Batman, and Aquaman on screens again as soon as possible. Fans have been wanting Batman and Wonder Woman again for years, and putting Aquaman back in the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Following the change in leadership, priorities for the DCU and future projects have shifted . David Ellison has expressed an interest in a fast-tracked Justice League , wanting Wonder Woman, Batman, and Aquaman on screens again as soon as possible. Fans have been wanting Batman and Wonder Woman again for years, and putting Aquaman back in the spotlight makes sense given the financial success of 2018’s Aquaman. With a focus on Justice League stories, there are few better places to look than the largely successful animated series Justice League Unlimited .

While the DCU has already carried over some villains from the show — see Lex Luthor in Superman or Amanda Waller in Creature Commandos — there’s still plenty left to make appearances. With Man of Tomorrow still on track to hit theaters, The People vs. Gorilla Grodd is still expected to introduce audiences to Gorilla Grodd. Gorilla Grodd made appearances in both Justice League and Justice League Unlimited, serving as a mastermind not only behind the Secret Society but also the Legion of Doom. Beyond Luthor and Grodd, DCU villains are still up in the air, but here are five solid picks for the Justice League to battle against.

Done dirty in Wonder Woman ‘84, the archeologist turned demigod Barbara Minerva deserves another shot in the DCU. In the DCAU canon, Barbara Minerva became the Cheetah when funding for her experiments ran out and she started testing on herself. Outcasted as a result, Cheetah turned to a life of crime. In Justice League and Justice League Unlimited , she mainly played a supporting role as one villain amongst a larger ensemble. Cheetah was part of both Lex Luthor’s Injustice Gang and Gorilla Grodd’s Legion of Doom.

Cheetah was largely in the background of episodes, with no strong individual plot of her own. Given the many retcons and alterations to the character , Cheetah could take a variety of forms in the DCU. She could be another monster that was created by experimentation like Matt Hagan in Clayface , or she could help bring in another god through her connection to Urzkartaga.

Darkseid first popped up in the extended animated universe in Superman: The Animated Series , but he's hardly just a Superman villain. He’d make appearances throughout Superman: The Animated Series along with an episode of Justice League prior to his resurrection during the first part of Justice League Unlimited ’s series finale. Due to the magnitude of the threat that Darkseid poses, the Justice League must temporarily ally with Lex Luthor and the Legion of Doom in order to bring Darkseid down.

Darkseid is an easy choice in terms of Justice League level threats, and was set to enter the DCU through the Mister Miracle animated series . With Josh Hutcherson and Mackenzie Davis lending their voices to the show for Mister Miracle and Big Barda, the show seemed well on its way, even though they hadn’t yet cast a voice actor for Darkseid. Given the duo’s ties to Apokolips, the show is a sensible way to introduce him to the DCU, especially since Darkseid has all the makings of a great big bad and would be wasted as a foe in a first or even second Justice League film.

As an evil sorceress from Arthurian times — and the half-sister of King Arthur — Morgaine le Fay had an interesting backstory with the formidable magic powers to match. Unlike the other villains that the Justice League faced throughout Justice League and Justice League Unlimited , Morgaine le Fay didn’t want power for herself, but rather for her son, Mordred. Morgaine le Fay may have only appeared in one episode of Justice League Unlimited, but it was one of the show’s most iconic episodes, and solidified her appearance on this list as a villain the Justice League could face. Magic is a route that hasn’t been explored much in DCU films yet and could make for different feeling films.

The Justice League Unlimited episode “Kid Stuff” saw Morgaine le Fay achieve her goal, but not in the way she intended. Le Fay gets her hands on the Amulet of First Magic which gives her and Mordred enough power to finally conquer the world. Although wanting him to have power, Morgaine le Fay is wary of him using the amulet because he’s too young — an action that causes him to snatch the amulet from her and wish that there were no more adults in the world. All adults are sent to a separate dimension, and Morgaine le Fay offers her services to the Justice League in order to defeat her son. In order to go back to the regular world, Le Fay turns Wonder Woman, Batman, Superman, and Green Lantern into children and wacky cartoon hijinks proceed from there.

2. Felix Faust More than just a tad pathetic, Faust is arguably one of the most memorable villains of the Justice League cartoons. Having made a Faustian bargain, Faust’s evil deeds are often in service of a higher power, such as Hades, putting him in direct conflict with Diana. Felix Faust very much felt like her villain, especially given the damage he did to Themyscira in “Paradise Lost”. Faust, under the tutelage of Hades, knew what Diana’s vulnerable spots were — her mother and sisters — and used them against her in order to get what he wanted. Unlike other heroes and their antagonists, the confrontation between Diana and Felix Faust had real consequences. Although acting in the island’s best interest, Diana’s choice to bring in the rest of the Justice League gets her exiled because she broke the “no men” rule that the island upheld.

The other Felix Faust story “The Balance” sees Diana returning to Themyscira once again in the aftermath of Felix Faust usurping Hades’s throne in Tartarus. Diana and Hawkgirl free Hades from his torment and together the three stop Faust. In the end, Diana’s welcomed back to Themyscria and Hades tasks himself with looking after the sole piece of Faust’s soul left. In the comics, Faust is frequently up to no good, often posing as other beings such as Dr. Fate and Deadman in order to achieve his ends. Faust could then be a compelling villain for the DCU and add complicated layers to what could otherwise be a straightforward story.

Brainiac is the type of villain that feels closer to a when, than an if, he’ll appear in the DCU. Although closely tied to Superman, Brainiac is a threat large enough to demand the attention of the whole Justice League. The Kryptonian AI — him originating from Krypton was a change made for Superman: The Animated Series in order to tie him closer to the Man of Steel  — continued his usual quest to destroy sources of knowledge after he attained the most valuable bits, putting him in direct conflict with the Man of Steel. 

Justice League Unlimited saw the character literally fuse with Lex Luthor becoming a hybrid of the two villains. Brainiac admits his role in curing Luthor’s kryptonite-induced cancer, showing just the tip of the iceberg of Brainiac’s power. Brainiac is presumed destroyed following Flash forcibly separating the two, but Gorilla Grodd reveals that he managed to save a fragment. Luthor then spends much of the third season of Unlimited obsessed with trying to merge with Brainiac again. Ultimately, Luthor fails in his quest and it is his unending efforts that bring forth Darkseid instead. Bringing Brainiac into the DCU is a no-brainer in terms of giving not only Superman another big bad, but also expands the universe given Brainiac’s plethora of knowledge and abilities. 

Which Justice League Unlimited villain are you still waiting for? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: Tim Burton’s Batman Plans Included a Radical Idea for Robin, And Toys Were Made Before It Was Scrapped
articles.summary: When Michael Keaton was cast as Batman in Tim Burton's 1989 film, everybody was shocked by the choice. Years later, many continue to say how great his performance was and place him high among the best actors to wear the cowl. Controversial casting choices are plentiful in comic book to movie adaptations, but there was […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google When Michael Keaton was cast as Batman in Tim Burton's 1989 film, everybody was shocked by the choice. Years later, many continue to say how great his performance was and place him high among the best actors to wear the cowl. Controversial casting choices are plentiful in comic book to movie adaptations, but there was one in this legendary DC franchise that would have shook the fandom to its core if it actually happened. Burton had the revolutionary idea of recasting Dick Grayson/ Robin as a Black character and felt that the perfect face for the iconic domino mask was Marlon Wayans.

The story behind this casting choice and what happened after a deal was reached is wild, and feels like it came straight out of a comic instead of real life. We all know that Wayans was never formally part of the franchise, but if rumor and innuendo are to be believed, he actually left a permanent mark on Batman that was a part of the childhood of many 90's kids and we didn't even know it. Even though Burton's unique proposal for Robin never made it into movie theaters, it may have made its way into the hand of any children who played with Batman action figures.

Tim Burton's Batman movie became one of the highest-grossing movies of 1989, making a sequel inevitable. There were a few things Burton wanted to accomplish in his first film that he tried to add into this second entry, including the introduction of Batman's sidekick, Robin. The character was removed from earlier drafts of the script since the producers felt there were too many characters already and not enough time to introduce The Boy Wonder, so Robin was sidelined until Batman Returns was in the works.

Meanwhile, Marlon Wayans was a newcomer to Hollywood , making his cinematic debut in his older brother Keenan's parody of 70's blaxploitation flicks, I'm Gonna Git You Sucka . His family had some star power attached to their names, but Marlon was a relative unknown at the time, and this anonymity appealed to Burton. The plan was to have Grayson be introduced in the sequel as himself, making a cameo as a mechanic who fixes the Batmobile. If a third film was made, Wayans would return and officially pick up the mantle as Robin.

Once again, Grayson was cut from Batman Returns due to the number of new characters introduced in the sequel. Despite this removal, Wayans was signed to be a part of the third movie in 1995, Batman Forever , but Tim Burton was ousted in favor of Joel Schumacher with the hopes that the picture would be less grim and easier to merchandise. As the film shifted in a different direction, Wayans was dropped and replaced by Chris O'Donnell. Luckily for Marlon, he was still paid for his nonappearance as the character and continues to receive royalties to this day for a movie he was never in. It doesn't completely remove the sting Wayans felt from losing out on this role, but it certainly helps the actor whose perspective on it has viewed the entire scenario in a more positive light.

"If Robin happened, I wouldn't be Marlon," the youngest sibling of the Wayans family explained during an interview with People Magazine earlier this year. "I might've blown up and become something different. I might've been Will Smith, but then I wouldn't be Marlon… Everything in my life has happened for a reason, and you may not understand it in the moment, but now that I'm 53, I can look back at that disappointed 19-year-old who got that part and was so hurt that it didn't happen, and I'm  glad  it didn't happen."

Officially and canonically, Marlon Wayans was never Robin in an onscreen role. However, many signs point to his version of the character being immortalized in plastic as an action figure. Production had already moved forward for toy manufacturer Kenner, who made the previous film's figures and were hard at work preparing for a new wave to coincide with the release of Batman Returns . According to the legends about this figure, Kenner didn't get the memo about Robin being cut from the script until it was too late. Instead, they continued working on the toys and allegedly repainted the product to a different skintone while keeping the sculpt unchanged.

Those who believe this theory point out the flat-top on Robin's head, which would make more sense for a Black character to have than a White one. However, some believe this was Kenner's interpretation of Norm Breyfogle's work on the character from the ongoing Batman comics or Tom Lyle's artwork from his 1991 Robin solo mini-series. Looking at the illustrations from both artists, the figure certainly shares inspiration from those appearances but the figure's hair is visibly taller and shaped differently than what Tim Drake typically had. No amount of gel would give Drake that kind of height, so there is likely some credence to this belief about Wayans being the basis of the toy.

Unfortunately, there has never been concrete evidence to separate what is fact from fiction, and this could be a case of inspiration coming from both the comic and movie sides. Fast forward to more recent events in the Batman '89 comic from 2021, and a character named Winston Drake debuted and went on to become Robin, fulfilling one of Burton's plans that never happened in the movies. As far as eight-year-old me is concerned, I'm still grateful that I had such a cool Robin figure to play with, and I appreciate the fact that whether it is or isn't Marlon Wayans, that guy had some real smarts to get paid for a role he never actually performed.

Would Marlon Wayans' career have been changed for the better or worse if he played Robin in a Batman movie? Join the conversation in the comments below and let us know how you feel about this decision.

articles.content:
The BBC has been told that its £500 million ($655M) savings plan will have a bigger impact on audiences than previous cuts, according to a new report.

The UK's National Audit Office (NAO) spending watchdog warned that the £500M target is a "significant step up" in savings efforts and will likely "result in more noticeable changes for audiences."

The BBC has been steadily announcing cuts in recent months, including plans to slash 2,000 jobs, close services like BBC Three, and cancel shows such as RuPaul's Drag Race UK . Related Stories News BBC Deputy Boss Questions Impact Of "Creative Choices Taken On West Coast Of United States" On UK Audiences News Melissa George Leading BBC-BritBox Detective Series 'The Loch Ness Mysteries'

The BBC has unveiled roughly £200M of the savings , which are required because the broadcaster has hemorrhaged more than two million licence fee payers since 2020. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

In a 52-page report, the NAO said: "Larger savings from scope reductions, delivered at a faster pace, could increase the risk of cumulative impacts on audiences, reputation and services, while potentially reducing the BBC’s capacity to manage further change."

The NAO warned that layoffs at the BBC could mean a brain drain that increases the risk of mistakes in content. In compiling the report, the BBC told the NAO that errors — such as Gaza: How to Survive a Warzone being narrated by the child of a Hamas minister — were not related to cuts.

The BBC acknowledged, however, that there is a "risk that further headcount reductions could result in the loss of staff with important skills and long-term experience of maintaining editorial integrity."

The NAO added: "The BBC’s efforts to achieve savings could reduce its data and cyber capability; delay investment in replacing ageing technology; and increase dependence on third-party suppliers."

The spending watchdog said the BBC should review whether its governance arrangements for delivering savings remain appropriate for the £500M plan.

articles.title: 5 Sci-Fi Movies That Were Too Ambitious For Their Own Good, Including Multiple Directors’ Pet Projects
articles.summary: The science fiction genre is one of the most consistently successful and popular in modern cinema, and each passing year offers exciting new releases. It's no secret that sci-fi sells, as some of the most iconic movie franchises are those that incorporate elements of science fiction into their stories. Many of the best sci-fi movies […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The science fiction genre is one of the most consistently successful and popular in modern cinema, and each passing year offers exciting new releases. It's no secret that sci-fi sells, as some of the most iconic movie franchises are those that incorporate elements of science fiction into their stories. Many of the best sci-fi movies are those that take place in awe-inspiring settings, imagining futuristic or mind-bending settings and scenarios for their stories to unfold in. In many ways, modern science fiction is as much about interesting concepts as it is about the execution, and sci-fi movies always seem to strive to deliver more of what fans seem to want.

Recently, we looked at fantasy movies that were too ambitious for their own good , and it turns out there are many sci-fi movies that fit the same profile. In their attempts to establish and deliver sprawling, compelling worlds filled with original ideas and unique characters, the following movies seemed to lose something that was far more important. Quantity should never outweigh quality, but that's something that these sci-fi movies all struggled with, and it ultimately backfired in pretty spectacular fashion.

Unfortunately, Jupiter Ascending is remembered mostly as a sci-fi movie so bad it's actually good , despite being the product of the minds behind The Matrix . The Wachowskis' attempt to deliver a completely original space opera fell short of expectations, although not necessarily for the reasons that seem obvious upon watching the movie. Admittedly, its lack of quality leaves a lot to be desired, but the reason the movie struggles is simply because it tries to do far too much all at once.

Introducing an elaborate galactic hierarchy of interplanetary politics, ancient alien dynasties, and an assortment of other sci-fi ideas all in a single movie saw Jupiter Ascending go from a movie with promise to a jumbled mess. Clearly intended to serve as the first chapter of an epic new space opera franchise, Jupiter Ascending instead fell flat, because the sheer amount of exposition required to make its story work made even its most promising elements collapse. In simple terms, the worldbuilding completely overwhelmed the narrative, and so much attention was given to establishing the bigger picture that the movie just wasn't very good on its own individual merit.

There aren't too many sci-fi movies that are terrible from beginning to end , but Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets is one of them. Remembered as the vanity project of the legendary sci-fi director Luc Besson, Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets served as an adaptation of the French comic book series Valérian and Laureline . In fairness to both Besson and the movie, in a visual sense it's both impressive and imaginative, although by almost every other conceivable metric, it's borderline unwatchable.

Filmmakers getting to realize their pet projects often leads to great things, but huge-budget sci-fi is always a risk, and Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets proves why. The priority seemed to be delivering an elaborate sci-fi world rather than telling an engaging story, and the total lack of chemistry between its stars, Dane DeHaan and Cara Delevingne, certainly didn't help. Had the movie been developed as a smaller-scale, more cohesive story first and a worldbuilding exercise second, it might have stood a chance, but ultimately, Besson's vision was far too ambitious for the movie to pull off.

Creating an ambitious sci-fi movie isn't always a case of bringing a fantastical world to life. 2004's Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow is remembered as a great sci-fi movie that continues to boast a cult following, but that doesn't mean that its ambitious nature didn't backfire. Starring Jude Law, Angelina Jolie, and Gwyneth Paltrow, the core idea behind the movie was to create a film that felt like a living illustration to serve as a love letter to the sci-fi serials and pulp magazines of the 1930s. Shot using an almost entirely digital environment, Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow is a film that largely lived up to the ambition behind it.

However, just because the movie achieved its goal and earned critical success, that doesn't mean its ambitious nature didn't backfire. General audiences found the visual style a little jarring, and many rejected the groundbreaking idea as a result. For all the ways that the experimental filmmaking technique made Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow stand out as a truly unique sci-fi film, it also alienated the wider audience that would have secured its success. The ambition behind the movie was, and remains to this day, commendable, but it ironically led to the movie struggling to achieve the recognition it deserved.

Across the genre's history, there have been a few painfully slow sci-fi movies that deserved to be much better than they were. 2012's Cloud Atlas is perhaps a prime example of this phenomenon, as the very notion of adapting David Mitchell's sci-fi novel onto the big screen was a more ambitious undertaking than most filmmakers would even want to consider. However, Tom Tykwer and the Wachowskis (yes, them again) sought to do just that, and the result is perhaps one of the purest examples of a movie too ambitious for its own good.

In order to explain why Cloud Atlas was such an ambitious adaptation, we need only to look at its story. Telling six stories across six different periods of human history, Cloud Atlas jumps between eras, making various complex links between its many characters. This not only led to its bloated three-hour runtime, but to a film that struggles to make any of its individual stories feel especially worthwhile. The overall product certainly isn't bad, and Cloud Atlas is considered a very rewarding watch by some, but the simple fact remains that turning Mitchell's novel into a big-budget sci-fi movie was an idea that was far too ambitious to ever really pull off.

Once upon a time, Zack Snyder was tipped to direct his own Star Wars movie. When the project fell through, Snyder opted instead to adapt his ideas into a space opera franchise of his own, and the result was Rebel Moon . Considering the way it came about, we can move past the derivative nature of its story, but what is particularly hard to reconcile is how overly ambitious Snyder was in his vision for the film. It's impossible to deny that Rebel Moon 's first chapter had both style and promise in spades, and it introduced many compelling characters that set up a sci-fi franchise worth getting excited for.

The problem with Rebel Moon - Part One: A Child of Fire is that it felt like a sci-fi movie trying too hard to be the next Star Wars . The first film had heaps of promise, but it felt like only part of a story, because so much time and attention was given to setting up the franchise that the film itself didn't really have a full plot. The sheer ambition of Rebel Moon is worth commending, because it epitomises Snyder's strengths as a filmmaker: it's sleek, eye-catching, and action-packed. However, in its attempts to set up a world which, admittedly, is incredibly engaging, the first film ironically ruined the franchise's chances for success by neglecting its own individual story.
